content: The text provided is a mix of fragmented references, study assessments, and methodological evaluations. 1. A study conducted in Tanzania in 2014, published in Social Science & Medicine, compared interventions within PMTCT (Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission) programs. However, it did not focus on the outcomes of interest. 2. Østergaard and Bula (2010) conducted a qualitative study in Malawi, exploring exclusive breastfeeding practices among HIV-positive mothers. The study highlighted the stigma associated with the term Nevirapine babies but did not provide detailed information on interventions or their outcomes. 3. Thairu et al. examined sociocultural influences on infant feeding decisions among HIV-infected women in rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The study compared cohort data with ethnographic findings but offered limited information on interventions and their outcomes. 4. Sellen, Wachira, and Gill (2007) investigated client experiences with counseling for safe infant feeding (SIF) in the context of PMTCT programs in Kenya. The study, published in FASEB Journal, lacked data on the impact of interventions on outcomes of interest. 5. Saloojee and Cooper (2010) reviewed infant feeding practices among HIV-positive mothers in a publication in Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition & Metabolic Care. This was a review article and not included in systematic reviews. 6. Bhandari, Kabir, and Salam (2008) discussed the integration of nutrition into maternal and child health programs, emphasizing the scaling up of exclusive breastfeeding. This review article was published in Maternal & Child Nutrition. 7. Rollins and Coovadia (2013) reviewed the relationship between breastfeeding and HIV transmission in developing countries, analyzing past, present, and future trends. This review article appeared in Current Opinion in HIV and AIDS. 8. Tomlinson et al. (2014) conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with low risk of bias. The study used computer randomization, blinded data collectors, and reported prespecified outcomes. Attrition rates were low, and the study appeared free from other sources of bias. 9. Bland (2008) conducted a cohort study assessing the representativeness of exposed and non-exposed groups, ascertainment of exposure, and comparability of cohorts. The study demonstrated adequate follow-up and accounted for all subjects, minimizing bias. 10. Iliff (2005) evaluated the representativeness of exposed cohorts, ascertainment of exposure, and comparability of cohorts. The study ensured adequate follow-up and accounted for all subjects, reducing the likelihood of bias. 11. Maziya (2009) assessed cohort studies for representativeness, ascertainment of exposure, and comparability. The study ensured adequate follow-up and accounted for all subjects, minimizing bias. 12. Piwowz (2005, 2007) conducted studies on cohort representativeness, ascertainment of exposure, and comparability. Both studies ensured adequate follow-up and accounted for all subjects, reducing the likelihood of bias. 13. Suryavanshi (2003) evaluated cohort studies for representativeness, ascertainment of exposure, and comparability. The study ensured adequate follow-up and accounted for all subjects, minimizing bias. 14. Thakwalakwa (2014) assessed cohort studies for representativeness, ascertainment of exposure, and comparability. The study ensured adequate follow-up and accounted for all subjects, reducing the likelihood of bias. 15. Bii (2008) conducted a cross-sectional study assessing sample representativeness, sample size, and non-respondents. The study controlled for confounding factors and used statistical tests to assess outcomes.
